mcqs.q: Medical research is best defined as:
opts: A systematic scientific investigation generating new knowledge that improves health
Routine application of textbook protocols to everyday patient care
The personal clinical experience a doctor gathers over years
A marketing process used to promote new pharmaceutical products
mcqs.explain: Research is a SYSTEMATIC, scientific investigation generating NEW knowledge — distinct from routine practice or opinion.

mcqs.q: The peptic-ulcer story is used to illustrate that:
opts: Medicine is dynamic — research proved H. pylori, not stress, causes peptic ulcer
Stress remains the confirmed primary cause of peptic ulcer disease
Textbook knowledge rarely needs revision once it is published
Antibiotics have no role in the management of peptic ulcer
mcqs.explain: Ulcers were blamed on stress until research identified Helicobacter pylori — a classic example that today's standard can become obsolete.

mcqs.q: Which is a listed AIM of medical research?
opts: Identify risk factors and develop diagnostic tests
Guarantee that every treatment will succeed
Replace the need for clinical judgment entirely
mcqs.explain: Aims include understanding diseases, identifying risk factors, developing diagnostics, evaluating treatments, and improving prevention/quality of life.

mcqs.q: 'Good research is objective, valid, reliable, reproducible and evidence-based.' The missing first characteristic is:
mcqs.explain: The list begins with Ethical, then Objective, Valid, Reliable, Reproducible, Evidence-based.

mcqs.q: Basic (laboratory) research is primarily aimed at:
opts: Understanding biological mechanisms (e.g. genetics, molecular biology, cell signaling)
Evaluating a new surgical technique in patients
Measuring hospital efficiency and patient satisfaction
Investigating a disease outbreak in a community
mcqs.explain: Basic research studies mechanisms in labs, animal and cell-culture models — not humans.

mcqs.q: Research conducted ON HUMANS to improve diagnosis and treatment (clinical trials, drug evaluation, surgical techniques) is called:
mcqs.explain: Clinical research is conducted on humans with the goal of improving diagnosis and treatment.

mcqs.q: Studying the DISTRIBUTION and DETERMINANTS of disease (risk factors, disease frequency, outbreak investigation) defines:
mcqs.explain: Epidemiology examines how disease is distributed and what determines it in populations.

mcqs.q: 'Bench to bedside' — turning laboratory discoveries into clinical practice — describes:
mcqs.explain: Translational research bridges laboratory science and clinical application ('bench to bedside').

mcqs.q: Hospital efficiency, healthcare quality and patient satisfaction are studied by:
mcqs.explain: Health-services research studies how healthcare is delivered.

mcqs.q: A study reporting the PREVALENCE of diabetes answers 'what is happening?' and is therefore:
mcqs.explain: Descriptive research answers 'what is happening?' (e.g. prevalence).

mcqs.q: Examining the ASSOCIATION between smoking and lung cancer ('why is it happening?') is:
mcqs.explain: Analytical research asks 'why?' — testing associations between exposures and outcomes.

mcqs.q: A randomized controlled trial, which answers 'what happens if we intervene?', is:
mcqs.explain: Experimental research (e.g. RCTs) tests the effect of a deliberate intervention.

mcqs.q: The correct FIRST step of the scientific method is:
mcqs.explain: Flow: Observation → Question → Hypothesis → Study design → Data collection → Analysis → Interpretation → Conclusion → Publication.

mcqs.q: In the smoking/lung-cancer example, a case-control study is analyzed by calculating the:
mcqs.explain: Case-control studies estimate association using the Odds Ratio.

mcqs.q: The NULL hypothesis (H₀) for smoking and lung cancer states:
opts: Smoking is NOT associated with lung cancer
mcqs.explain: H₀ is the 'no association' statement; H₁ (alternative) states smoking increases risk.

mcqs.q: In the 10-step research process, the step immediately AFTER identifying the research problem is:
mcqs.explain: Order: identify problem → literature review → research question → hypothesis → design → collect → analyze → interpret → manuscript → publish.

mcqs.q: In the FINER criteria for a good research question, 'N' stands for:
mcqs.explain: FINER = Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant.

mcqs.q: In FINER, the 'E' stands for:
mcqs.explain: FINER: Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant.

mcqs.q: In the PICO framework, the letter 'C' represents:
mcqs.explain: PICO = Patient/Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome.

mcqs.q: 'In hypertensive adults, does Drug A compared with Drug B reduce stroke incidence?' — 'reduce stroke incidence' is the:
mcqs.explain: The outcome is what you measure — here, stroke incidence.

mcqs.q: 'First, do no harm' corresponds to which ethical principle?
mcqs.explain: Non-maleficence = avoid harm; beneficence = maximize benefit.

mcqs.q: Voluntary participation and informed consent fall under the principle of:
mcqs.explain: Respect for persons covers voluntary participation and informed consent.

mcqs.q: Fair participant selection and equal treatment express the principle of:
mcqs.explain: Justice = fairness in who is enrolled and how they are treated.

mcqs.q: Approval from an Institutional Review Board (IRB)/Ethics Committee is required:
opts: Only after the data have been analyzed
Only when the study is submitted for publication
mcqs.explain: Every human-research project needs IRB/ethics approval BEFORE recruitment.

mcqs.q: Which is an element participants must be told for INFORMED CONSENT?
opts: Their right to withdraw at any time
The researcher's personal income from the study
The names of all other participants
A guarantee of a successful outcome
mcqs.explain: Consent covers purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality and the right to withdraw.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognized CHALLENGE in medical research?
mcqs.explain: Challenges include limited funding, small samples, bias, confounding, ethical issues, missing data and poor design.

mcqs.q: Which is listed as a FUTURE DIRECTION for medical research?
mcqs.explain: Future directions: AI, big data, precision medicine, genomics, wearables, digital health, telemedicine.

mcqs.q: Evidence-Based Medicine is the integration of:
opts: Best research evidence + clinical expertise + patient values
mcqs.explain: Without research, medicine becomes opinion-based; EBM integrates evidence, expertise and patient values.

mcqs.q: Which text is listed as suggested reading on the ethical principles for research on human subjects?
opts: The World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki
Greenhalgh's How to Read a Paper
mcqs.explain: The other three cover study design, critical appraisal and epidemiology respectively.

mcqs.q: Which characteristic of good research means the study can be repeated by others with the same result?
mcqs.explain: Good research is also ethical, objective, valid, reliable and evidence-based.

mcqs.q: Aspirin reducing mortality after myocardial infarction is given as an example of research that:
opts: Improves patient care, on which evidence-based medicine depends
mcqs.explain: Immunotherapy, gene therapy and monoclonal antibodies are the examples of developing new treatments.

mcqs.q: Vaccines, smoking-cessation programmes and cancer screening are given as examples of research contributing to:
mcqs.explain: Cost-effectiveness and which screening saves more lives are the healthcare-systems examples.

saqs.q: Define 'medical research' and list any three of its aims.
saqs.a: MEDICAL RESEARCH — a systematic scientific investigation designed to generate new knowledge that improves health and healthcare. Aims: understand diseases · identify risk factors · develop diagnostic tests · evaluate treatments · improve prevention · improve quality of life.

ans.text: A systematic scientific investigation designed to generate new knowledge that improves health and healthcare.

saqs.q: Name the five TYPES of medical research and give one example/feature of each.
saqs.a: BASIC/LABORATORY — mechanisms (genetics, cell signaling). CLINICAL — on humans (trials, drug evaluation). EPIDEMIOLOGICAL — distribution and determinants (risk factors, outbreaks). TRANSLATIONAL — 'bench to bedside'. HEALTH-SERVICES — healthcare delivery (efficiency, quality, satisfaction).

head: Type
Example / feature
rows: on humans — clinical trials, drug evaluation
distribution and determinants — risk factors, outbreaks

saqs.q: Differentiate descriptive, analytical and experimental research by the question each answers, with an example.
saqs.a: DESCRIPTIVE — 'what is happening?' (prevalence of diabetes). ANALYTICAL — 'why is it happening?' (smoking–lung cancer association). EXPERIMENTAL — 'what happens if we intervene?' (randomized controlled trials).

saqs.q: What does PICO stand for? Write a PICO question using Drug A vs Drug B for stroke prevention in hypertensive adults.
saqs.a: P = Patient/Population · I = Intervention · C = Comparison · O = Outcome. 'In hypertensive adults (P), does Drug A (I) compared with Drug B (C) reduce stroke incidence (O)?'

ans.text: In hypertensive adults (P), does Drug A (I) compared with Drug B (C) reduce stroke incidence (O)?

saqs.q: List the four core ethical principles of medical research and state four items an informed-consent discussion must cover.
saqs.a: PRINCIPLES — respect for persons, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice. CONSENT must cover purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, confidentiality, and the right to withdraw.

saqs.q: A researcher notices many smokers develop lung cancer. Outline how they would apply the scientific method, including H₀ and H₁.
saqs.a: Observation → question → hypothesis (H₁ smoking increases lung-cancer risk; H₀ no association) → study design (case-control) → data collection → analysis (Odds Ratio) → interpretation → conclusion (accept/reject H₀) → publication.

steps: Hypothesis — H₁: smoking increases lung-cancer risk · H₀: no association
